title: Everything you need to know about Fine-tuning and Merging LLMs: Maxime Labonne

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is SFT, DPO, LoRA, QLoRA, and model merging—all post-training adaptation methods covered by this category's inclusion criteria. The content covers general-purpose LLM fine-tuning and merging techniques applicable across all application verticals. The talk centers on post-training (SFT, preference alignment, model merging), with secondary coverage of evaluation frameworks and SFT data preparation pipelines. Prerequisites include LLM training fundamentals and prompt engineering familiarity, and the content covers intermediate techniques like LoRA, QLoRA, DPO, and FrankenMoE merging. summary: Maxime Labonne frames the LLM training lifecycle in three stages: pre-training (next token prediction on raw text yields a base model), supervised fine-tuning (instruction-answer pairs yield an instruction-following model), and preference alignment (human preferences yield a chat model). He recommends starting with prompt engineering and a robust evaluation framework before considering fine-tuning, noting that non-technical drivers—control and customizability per an a16z report—also push enterprises toward open-source fine-tuning. He surveys fine-tuning libraries: TRL (Hugging Face), Axolotl (YAML configs), and LLaMA-Factory (graphical interface). For SFT, he shows the instruction-output format with masked context and output-only training loss, noting most SFT datasets use synthetic data from frontier models. For preference alignment, DPO is the most popular method, using chosen/rejected answer pairs to steer model probabilities. He identifies three SFT data quality pillars—accuracy, diversity, and complexity (forcing reasoning via Chain of Thought)—and recommends a pipeline combining open-source datasets, deduplication, quality filtering (rule-based, reward models, LLM-as-judge), and data exploration. For techniques, he compares full fine-tuning (best performance, most expensive), LoRA (freezes base weights, trains low-rank adapters), and QLoRA (adds 4-bit quantization for lower VRAM at some performance cost). He then covers model merging—combining weights of fine-tuned models without GPUs—which dominates the Open LLM Leaderboard top 10 for 7B models. Beyond SLERP and TIES, he presents pass-through merging (concatenating layers from different or the same LLM, called self-merge), illustrated by a Meta Llama 3 30B model created by repeating 10 layers six times with no fine-tuning, which excelled at creative writing. He also introduces Mixture of Experts via merging (FrankenMoE), extracting FFN layers from different fine-tuned models and adding a router initialized via positive prompts. His Beyond model combined chat, code, roleplay, and math models, outperforming source models on benchmarks. He notes SLERP and DARE yield better performance gains than MoE merging, which remains more experimental. He concludes by directing viewers to his LLM Course on GitHub.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Maxime Labonne introduces himself as a Staff ML Scientist at Liquid AI, Google Developer Expert, creator of the LLM Course on GitHub, open-source contributor, and author of a book on graph neural networks.

sections.title: LLM Training Lifecycle
sections.summary: Describes three training stages: pre-training (raw text, next token prediction → base model), supervised fine-tuning (Q&A pairs → instruction-following model), and preference alignment (human preferences → chat model). Base models autocomplete questions rather than answering them.

sections.title: When to Use Fine-tuning
sections.summary: Recommends starting with prompt engineering and a robust evaluation framework (accuracy, custom benchmarks, open-source benchmarks, cost, latency). If prompt engineering is insufficient and an instruction dataset can be created, fine-tuning is an option. Non-technical driver: a16z report shows enterprises value open source for control and customizability.

sections.title: Fine-tuning Libraries
sections.summary: Mentions TRL (Hugging Face, built on Transformers, easy to use), Axolotl (versatile, YAML configs), and LLaMA-Factory (graphical interface).

sections.title: SFT Format and Data
sections.summary: Shows SFT sample with system prompt (steering behavior), user prompt (task), and output. Training is on outputs only with rest masked as context. Notes most SFT datasets use synthetic data generated by frontier models, which is perfectly fine.

sections.title: Preference Alignment (DPO)
sections.summary: Introduces DPO as the most popular preference alignment method alongside PPO, KTO, IPO. Format uses instruction with chosen and rejected answers. Goal: make the trained model assign higher probability to chosen answers than the untrained version. Can enforce safety or boost general performance.

sections.title: Creating SFT Datasets
sections.summary: Defines three quality features: accuracy (factual correctness, no typos), diversity (topic and style coverage), and complexity (Chain of Thought reasoning, tasks forcing reasoning beyond simple QA). Recommends pipeline: start with open-source datasets, apply deduplication (exact and fuzzy), quality filtering (rule-based, reward models, LLM-as-judge), and data exploration (topic clustering). Iterate based on insights.

sections.title: SFT Techniques
sections.summary: Compares full fine-tuning (best performance, least efficient), LoRA (freezes pre-trained weights, adds adapter matrices A and B to targeted layers, trains subset of parameters), and QLoRA (quantizes base model to 4-bit for lower VRAM, but degrades performance).

sections.title: Hyperparameters
sections.summary: Key hyperparameters: learning rate (model-dependent, push as high as possible until loss explodes then reduce), number of epochs (depends on dataset size), sequence length (trades off with batch size for VRAM), batch size (maximize GPU utilization), and LoRA rank (easy to fine-tune).

sections.title: Model Merging Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces model merging: combining weights of different fine-tuned models without GPUs, producing excellent results—entire top 8-10 of Open LLM Leaderboard for 7B models are merges. Recommends mergekit library. Mentions SLERP (spherical linear interpolation, two models, per-layer factors) and TIES (pruning for parameter redundancy reduction). Shows family tree of merged models.

sections.title: Advanced Merging: Pass-through and FrankenMoE
sections.summary: Covers additional merging techniques. Pass-through concatenates layers from different or the same LLM (self-merge); example Meta Llama 3 30B Instruct repeated 10 layers six times from Llama 3 70B with no fine-tuning, excelling at creative writing. FrankenMoE extracts FFN layers from different fine-tuned models, adds a router initialized via positive prompts (chat, code, roleplay, math models for the Beyond model). Notes SLERP and DARE yield better performance than MoE merging, which is more experimental. Beyond model outperformed its source models on benchmarks. Concludes by directing viewers to the LLM Course on GitHub.
